reminder: Every map factors as a left map then a right map, and each class is exactly the maps that lift against the other.
definition: A weak factorization system $(L,R)$ on a [category](c:category) is a pair of classes of morphisms such that every morphism $f$ is a [composition](c:composition) $f=r\circ l$ with $l\in L$ and $r\in R$. In addition, $L$ is exactly the class of morphisms with the [left lifting property](c:has-lifting-property) against every morphism of $R$, and $R$ is exactly the class with the right lifting property against every morphism of $L$.
examples: In the category of sets, the injections and the surjections form a weak factorization system: a map $f:X\to Y$ factors as $X\to X\sqcup Y\to Y$.
In every model category, the pair (cofibrations, acyclic fibrations) and the pair (acyclic cofibrations, fibrations) are weak factorization systems.

Non-example: in the category of sets, take both classes to be the injections; the map from a two-point set to a point does not factor as two injections, so this pair is not a weak factorization system.

steps: Take an [orthogonal factorization system](c:orthogonal-factorization-system) $(E,M)$ on a category: every map factors as $m\circ e$ with $e\in E$ and $m\in M$, and each square from $E$ to $M$ has a unique lift.
A unique lift is in particular a lift, so every map of $E$ has the left lifting property against $M$.
If a map $f$ lifts against $M$, then factoring $f=m\circ e$ shows that $f$ is a retract of $e$, so $f\in E$.
So each class is the lifting complement of the other, and $(E,M)$ is a weak factorization system whose lifts happen to be unique.
links.why: Every fact about weak factorization systems, such as the retract argument, applies to every orthogonal factorization system.

reminder: In a well-founded relation, a property that passes from all predecessors of $x$ to $x$ holds for every element.
definition: Let $\prec$ be a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation) on a [set](c:set) $X$ and let $P$ be a property of elements of $X$. Well-founded induction says: if $P(x)$ follows from $P(y)$ for all $y\prec x$, for every $x\in X$, then $P(x)$ holds for all $x\in X$.
examples: On the natural numbers with $m\prec n$ meaning $m<n$, well-founded induction is strong induction.
On finite lists with $s\prec t$ meaning that $s$ is a proper tail of $t$, it proves facts about lists by induction on the length.
On the terms of a rewriting system that has no infinite reduction chain, with $s\prec t$ meaning that $t$ rewrites to $s$ in one step, it gives induction along reductions.
Non-example: on the integers with $<$, the property $n\ge0$ passes from the predecessors of each $n$ to $n$, yet it fails at $-1$; this is because $<$ is not well founded on the integers.

steps: Take an ordinal $\gamma$ with the relation $\alpha\prec\beta$ meaning $\alpha<\beta$.
Every nonempty set of ordinals has a least element, so this relation is a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation).
Well-founded induction for this relation says: if $P(\beta)$ follows from $P(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha<\beta$, then $P$ holds on all of $\gamma$.
This statement is [transfinite induction](c:transfinite-induction) on $\gamma$.
links.why: Induction along any well-founded relation, not only along ordinals, is as valid as transfinite induction.

reminder: A well order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element.
definition: A well order on a [set](c:set) $S$ is a [total order](c:total-order) $\le$ on $S$ such that every nonempty [subset](c:subset) of $S$ has a least element.
examples: The natural numbers with the usual order are well ordered; $0$ is the least element of every set that contains it.
Every finite total order is a well order, and so is every ordinal, such as $\omega+1=\{0,1,2,\dots,\omega\}$.
Non-example: the integers with the usual order are not well ordered, because the subset of negative integers has no least element.

steps: Take a well order $\le$ on a set $S$; by definition it is a [total order](c:total-order).
So every fact about total orders applies to $\le$.
The well order adds the condition that every nonempty subset has a least element.
This condition rules out every infinite strictly descending sequence $a_0>a_1>\cdots$, because $\{a_n\}$ would have no least element.
links.why: A well order keeps all the structure of a total order and adds a base case for induction.

steps: Take a well order $\le$ and let $a<b$ mean $a\le b$ and $a\ne b$.
Every nonempty subset has a least element, and a least element is minimal for $<$.
So $<$ is a [well-founded relation](c:well-founded-relation).
The well order adds that $<$ is also total, so any two elements are comparable.
links.why: Well-founded induction works along every well order, in particular along the natural numbers and the ordinals.

reminder: In a well-quasi-order, every infinite sequence has two indices $i<j$ with $x_i\le x_j$.
definition: A well-quasi-order is a [preorder](c:is-preorder) $(P,\le)$ in which every infinite [sequence](c:sequence) $x_0,x_1,\dots$ has indices $i<j$ with $x_i\le x_j$. Equivalently, $P$ has no infinite strictly descending sequence and no infinite [antichain](c:antichain).
examples: The natural numbers with the usual order form a well-quasi-order.
The pairs of natural numbers with the product order form a well-quasi-order; this is Dickson's lemma.
Finite trees ordered by homeomorphic embedding form a well-quasi-order; this is Kruskal's tree theorem.
Non-example: the natural numbers with divisibility are not a well-quasi-order, because the primes form an infinite antichain.

steps: Take a [well order](c:well-order) $\le$ on $P$ and an infinite sequence $x_0,x_1,\dots$ in $P$.
The set of values $\{x_n\}$ is nonempty, so it has a least element $x_m$.
Then $x_m\le x_{m+1}$, so the indices $m<m+1$ satisfy the condition of a well-quasi-order.
So every well order is a well-quasi-order; the converse fails, because a well-quasi-order need not be total.
links.why: A theorem about well-quasi-orders applies at once to every well-ordered set.

steps: Take a well-quasi-order $(P,\le)$.
By definition $\le$ is reflexive and transitive, so $(P,\le)$ is a [preorder](c:is-preorder).
The well-quasi-order adds that every infinite sequence has indices $i<j$ with $x_i\le x_j$.
links.why: A well-quasi-order keeps the facts about preorders and also gives each upward closed set a finite set of generators.

reminder: Wiener measure is the probability measure on continuous paths that makes the coordinate process a Brownian motion.
definition: Wiener measure is the [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $W$ on the space of [continuous](c:continuous-function) paths $\omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^n$ with $\omega(0)=0$ under which the coordinate process $t\mapsto\omega(t)$ is a [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion). That is, the increments over disjoint time intervals are [independent](c:independent-increments), and the increment over $[s,t]$ has a [Gaussian distribution](c:gaussian-probability-distribution) with mean $0$ and covariance $(t-s)I$.
examples: Under Wiener measure on paths in $\mathbb R$, the value $\omega(t)$ at a fixed time $t>0$ has the normal distribution with mean $0$ and variance $t$.
The set of paths with $\omega(1)>0$ has Wiener measure $\tfrac12$, by the symmetry of the normal distribution.
The Wiener integral of a functional $F$ is $\int F(\omega)\,dW(\omega)$, the Lebesgue integral of $F$ with respect to $W$.
Non-example: a measure that is concentrated on differentiable paths is not Wiener measure, because Brownian paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable.

steps: Take Wiener measure $W$ on the Banach space of continuous paths $\omega:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ with $\omega(0)=0$.
Finitely many values $\omega(t_1),\dots,\omega(t_k)$ are jointly Gaussian with covariance $\min(t_i,t_j)$.
Every continuous linear functional of a path is a limit of combinations of such values, so it is a Gaussian random variable.
So $W$ is a [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) with mean $0$ and covariance $\min(s,t)$.
links.why: Facts about Gaussian measures, such as the Cameron-Martin space of shifts, apply to Wiener measure.

reminder: ZF is the first-order theory of sets given by the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms, without the axiom of choice.
definition: ZF set theory is the theory in [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) with one binary relation symbol $\in$ whose axioms are extensionality, foundation, pairing, union, [power set](c:power-set), [infinity](c:axiom-of-infinity), and the [axiom schemas](c:axiom-schema) of separation and [replacement](c:axiom-of-replacement). The axiom of choice is not an axiom of ZF.
examples: ZF proves that every set has a power set and that the ordinals are well ordered.
Gödel's constructible universe $L$ is a model of ZF; in fact it satisfies the axiom of choice as well.
If ZF is consistent, then ZF does not prove the axiom of choice, by Cohen's forcing method.
Non-example: naive set theory, where every property defines a set, is not ZF; it proves a contradiction (Russell's set), which the separation schema blocks.

steps: Take a model $M$ of [ZFC](c:zfc).
ZFC has all axioms of ZF and one more, the axiom of choice, so $M$ satisfies every axiom of ZF.
Hence every model of ZFC is a model of ZF.
So every theorem of ZF is also a theorem of ZFC, and ZF is the weaker theory.
links.why: A result proved in ZF holds in every model of ZFC, and it needs no choice.

reminder: ZFC is Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice added.
definition: ZFC is the theory in [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) whose axioms are the axioms of [ZF set theory](c:zf-set-theory) together with the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). The axiom of choice says that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
examples: ZFC proves that every vector space has a basis and that every set can be well ordered.
Most of analysis and algebra can be formalized in ZFC.
If ZFC is consistent, it neither proves nor refutes the continuum hypothesis, by Gödel and Cohen.
Non-example: ZF without the axiom of choice is not ZFC; if ZF is consistent, it does not prove that every set can be well ordered.

steps: Start from the axioms of [ZF set theory](c:zf-set-theory).
Add the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) as one more axiom.
Every model of the larger theory satisfies the axioms of ZF, so it is a model of ZF.
The axiom of choice is the only condition that ZFC adds to ZF.
links.why: Every theorem of ZF holds in ZFC, so a proof in ZF needs no new check.

reminder: A zigzag persistence module is a diagram of vector spaces whose linear maps may point in either direction along a line.
definition: A zigzag persistence module is a [diagram](c:diagram) of [vector spaces](c:vector-space) and linear maps over a [zigzag](c:zigzag) $V_0\leftrightarrow V_1\leftrightarrow\cdots\leftrightarrow V_n$, where each arrow points left or right. A finite-dimensional zigzag persistence module is a direct sum of [indecomposable](c:indecomposable-object) interval modules, and each one records a feature that is born and dies along the zigzag.
examples: The diagram $k\to k\leftarrow k$ with identity maps is a zigzag persistence module; it is one interval module over the whole zigzag.
Take the homology of spaces joined by inclusions $X_0\hookrightarrow X_1\hookleftarrow X_2\hookrightarrow X_3$; this gives a zigzag persistence module.
An ordinary persistence module $V_0\to V_1\to\cdots\to V_n$ is the special case where every arrow points right.
Non-example: the diagram with maps $V_0\to V_1$, $V_0\to V_2$ and $V_0\to V_3$ has a star shape, not a line, so it is not a zigzag persistence module.

steps: Take a zigzag shape: a line with $n+1$ vertices and one arrow on each edge, pointing left or right.
View this shape as a category generated by those arrows.
A [diagram](c:diagram) of vector spaces of this shape gives a vector space at each vertex and a linear map at each arrow.
A zigzag persistence module is such a diagram; the special case adds that the shape is a zigzag.
links.why: General tools for diagrams, such as limits and colimits, apply to zigzag persistence modules.

reminder: An A-infinity algebra is a chain complex with a product that is associative only up to coherent higher homotopies.
definition: An $A_\infty$-algebra is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $(A,m_1)$ with [multilinear](c:multilinear-map) operations $m_n:A^{\otimes n}\to A$ of degree $2-n$ for $n\ge2$, which satisfy the Stasheff identities. The first identities say that $m_1$ is a derivation of $m_2$ and that $m_2$ is [associative](c:associativity) up to the [homotopy](c:homotopy) $m_3$.
examples: Every differential graded associative algebra is an $A_\infty$-algebra with $m_n=0$ for $n\ge3$.
The chains on a loop space $\Omega X$, with concatenation of loops, form an $A_\infty$-algebra, because concatenation is associative only up to homotopy.
The cohomology of a differential graded algebra carries an $A_\infty$-structure with $m_1=0$ that is quasi-isomorphic to the algebra, by Kadeishvili's theorem.
Non-example: the octonions with $m_1=0$, $m_2$ the product and $m_n=0$ for $n\ge3$ are not an $A_\infty$-algebra, because the product is not associative and $m_3=0$ gives no homotopy.

steps: Take a [differential graded algebra](c:differential-graded-algebra) $(A,d,\cdot)$.
Set $m_1=d$, let $m_2$ be the product, and set $m_n=0$ for $n\ge3$.
The Stasheff identities reduce to the Leibniz rule for $d$ and to strict associativity of the product.
So $A$ is an $A_\infty$-algebra whose higher homotopies are all zero.
links.why: Every tool for $A_\infty$-algebras, such as the transfer of structure along a quasi-isomorphism, applies to differential graded algebras.

reminder: An accessible functor between accessible categories preserves $\kappa$-filtered colimits for some regular cardinal $\kappa$.
definition: Let $\kappa$ be a [regular cardinal](c:is-regular). A [functor](c:functor) $F:C\to D$ is $\kappa$-accessible if $C$ and $D$ are $\kappa$-[accessible categories](c:accessible-category) and $F$ preserves $\kappa$-[filtered colimits](c:filtered-colimit). The functor $F$ is accessible if it is $\kappa$-accessible for some regular cardinal $\kappa$.
examples: The forgetful functor from groups to sets preserves filtered colimits, so it is $\omega$-accessible.
Every left adjoint between locally presentable categories preserves all colimits, so it is accessible.
The identity functor of an accessible category is accessible.
Non-example: the covariant power set functor $\mathcal P:\mathrm{Set}\to\mathrm{Set}$ is not accessible, because no regular cardinal $\kappa$ makes it preserve $\kappa$-filtered colimits.

steps: Take an accessible functor $F:C\to D$ between accessible categories.
By definition $F$ is a [functor](c:functor) from $C$ to $D$.
The accessible case adds that $F$ preserves $\kappa$-filtered colimits for some regular cardinal $\kappa$.
This condition is what keeps constructions such as the small object argument under control.
links.why: An accessible functor has a size bound on its behavior, so it can be iterated transfinitely.

reminder: A point is an accumulation point of a set when every neighborhood of it contains another point of the set.
definition: Let $S$ be a [subset](c:subset) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. A point $x\in X$ is an accumulation point of $S$ if every [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$ contains a point of $S$ that is different from $x$.
examples: The point $0$ is an accumulation point of $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ in $\mathbb R$.
Every real number is an accumulation point of $\mathbb Q$ in $\mathbb R$, and every point of $[0,1]$ is an accumulation point of $(0,1)$.
Non-example: the point $1$ belongs to $\{1/n:n\ge1\}$ but is not an accumulation point, because the neighborhood $(0.9,1.1)$ contains no other point of the set.

reminder: The Adams operation $\psi^k$ is the natural ring homomorphism of K-theory that sends a line bundle $L$ to $L^{\otimes k}$.
definition: For an integer $k\ge0$, the Adams operation $\psi^k$ is the unique natural [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) $K(X)\to K(X)$ on [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory) that sends each complex line bundle $L$ to $L^{\otimes k}$. It is computed from the exterior power operations of the [$\lambda$-ring](c:lambda-ring) $K(X)$ by Newton's formulas.
examples: The operation $\psi^0$ sends each class to its rank, and $\psi^1$ is the identity.
For a vector bundle $E$, $\psi^2(E)=E\otimes E-2\Lambda^2E$.
On the reduced K-theory of the sphere $S^{2n}$, the operation $\psi^k$ acts as multiplication by $k^n$.
Non-example: the map $E\mapsto E\otimes E$ is not an Adams operation, because it is not additive: $(E\oplus F)^{\otimes2}$ contains the cross term $2\,E\otimes F$.

steps: Take the functor $X\mapsto K(X)$ from spaces to rings, which is a [cohomology](c:cohomology) theory in degree $0$.
An Adams operation $\psi^k$ is a natural transformation from this functor to itself.
A natural transformation of a cohomology theory to itself is a [cohomology operation](c:cohomology-operation).
The Adams operation adds that each $\psi^k$ is a ring homomorphism with $\psi^k(L)=L^{\otimes k}$ on line bundles.
links.why: General facts about cohomology operations apply to Adams operations, which are the ring-valued ones with the best properties.

reminder: The adjacency matrix of a graph has entry 1 in position $(i,j)$ when vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent, and 0 otherwise.
definition: Let $G$ be a [graph](c:graph) with [vertices](c:vertex) $v_1,\dots,v_n$. Its adjacency matrix is the $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ with $A_{ij}=1$ when $v_i$ and $v_j$ are joined by an [edge](c:edge) and $A_{ij}=0$ otherwise; for a multigraph, $A_{ij}$ counts the edges.
examples: The path $1-2-3$ has the adjacency matrix with rows $(0,1,0)$, $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,0)$.
The complete graph $K_n$ has adjacency matrix $J-I$, where $J$ is the matrix of all ones.
The entry $(A^k)_{ij}$ counts the walks of length $k$ from $v_i$ to $v_j$.
Non-example: the incidence matrix has one row per vertex and one column per edge, so it is not the adjacency matrix, which has vertices on both sides.

reminder: An affine group scheme is a group object in the category of affine schemes.
definition: An affine group scheme over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $k$ is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of [affine schemes](c:affine-scheme) over $k$. Equivalently, it is $\operatorname{Spec}A$ for a commutative [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) $A$ over $k$.
examples: The additive group $\mathbb G_a=\operatorname{Spec}k[x]$, with comultiplication $x\mapsto x\otimes1+1\otimes x$.
The multiplicative group $\mathbb G_m=\operatorname{Spec}k[x,x^{-1}]$, with comultiplication $x\mapsto x\otimes x$.
The general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n=\operatorname{Spec}k[x_{ij},\det{}^{-1}]$.
Non-example: an elliptic curve over a field is a group scheme, but it is projective and not affine, so it is not an affine group scheme.

steps: Take an affine group scheme $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$ over $k$.
It is a group object in the category of affine schemes over $k$, which sits inside the category of all schemes over $k$.
So $G$ is a group object in schemes over $k$, that is, a [group scheme](c:group-scheme).
The affine case adds that the underlying scheme is affine, so the Hopf algebra $A$ determines $G$.
links.why: Every fact about group schemes applies to affine group schemes, which have the extra description by Hopf algebras.

steps: Take a [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) $G$ over a field $k$, a closed subgroup of some $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
Its coordinate ring $A$ is a quotient of $k[x_{ij},\det{}^{-1}]$ by a Hopf ideal.
So $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is an affine group scheme over $k$.
The linear algebraic group adds that $A$ is finitely generated over $k$, and reduced in the classical definition.
links.why: Results for affine group schemes apply to linear algebraic groups, and they also cover non-reduced and infinite-type cases.

reminder: An affine open cover of a scheme is a family of open affine subschemes whose union is the whole scheme.
definition: An affine open cover of a [scheme](c:scheme) $X$ is a family of [open](c:open-set) subschemes $U_i$ with $\bigcup_iU_i=X$ such that each $U_i$ is an [affine scheme](c:affine-scheme).
examples: The projective line $\mathbb P^1_k$ is covered by the two affine opens $D_+(x_0)\cong\mathbb A^1$ and $D_+(x_1)\cong\mathbb A^1$.
If $(f_1,\dots,f_r)$ is the unit ideal of $A$, the basic open sets $D(f_i)$ form an affine open cover of $\operatorname{Spec}A$.
Every scheme has an affine open cover, because by definition each point has an affine open neighborhood.
Non-example: the punctured plane $\mathbb A^2\setminus\{0\}$ covers itself, but it is not affine, so the family with this one member is not an affine open cover.

steps: Take an affine open cover $\{U_i\}$ of a scheme $X$.
Each $U_i$ is open in $X$, and the union of the $U_i$ is $X$.
So $\{U_i\}$ is an [open cover](c:open-cover) of the underlying space of $X$.
The affine case adds that each $U_i$ is an affine scheme, so it is the spectrum of a ring.
links.why: Facts about open covers apply, and each piece can be studied by commutative algebra.

reminder: An affine variety is the set of common zeros in affine space of a set of polynomials.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field), usually [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field). An affine variety is the [zero locus](c:zero-locus) $V(S)\subseteq\mathbb A^n_k$ of a set $S$ of [polynomials](c:polynomial) in $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, with the induced Zariski topology; many authors also require it to be irreducible.
examples: The parabola $V(y-x^2)$ in the plane $\mathbb A^2$.
The whole space $\mathbb A^n=V(0)$, and every point $V(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)$.
The circle $V(x^2+y^2-1)$ in $\mathbb A^2$ over $\mathbb C$.
Non-example: the set $\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb A^1(\mathbb C)$ is not a zero locus, because a nonzero polynomial in one variable has finitely many roots.

steps: Take an affine variety $X$ with its sheaf of regular functions.
The open set $X$ is itself an affine variety, and it covers $X$.
An [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) is a separated space covered by open affine varieties, and affine varieties are separated.
So $X$ is an algebraic variety; general varieties are glued from affine pieces.
links.why: Local questions about any variety reduce to questions about affine varieties and polynomial rings.

reminder: An affinoid algebra is a quotient of a Tate algebra of convergent power series over a complete non-archimedean field.
definition: Let $k$ be a complete non-archimedean valued field. An affinoid algebra over $k$ is a [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) of the form $T_n/I$, where $T_n=k\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ is the [Tate algebra](c:tate-algebra) of [power series](c:formal-power-series) whose coefficients tend to $0$, $I$ is an [ideal](c:ideal), and the [norm](c:norm) is the quotient norm.
examples: The Tate algebra $k\langle x\rangle$, which is the algebra of functions on the closed unit disc.
The algebra $k\langle x,y\rangle/(xy-\pi)$ with $0<|\pi|<1$, which is the algebra of functions on the annulus $|\pi|\le|x|\le1$.
The algebra $\mathbb Q_p\langle x\rangle$ of series $\sum a_nx^n$ with $a_n\in\mathbb Q_p$ and $a_n\to0$.
Non-example: the algebra of bounded holomorphic functions on the complex unit disc is a Banach algebra but not an affinoid algebra, because $\mathbb C$ is archimedean.

steps: Take an affinoid algebra $A=T_n/I$ over a complete non-archimedean field $k$.
The Tate algebra is complete for the Gauss norm, and the ideal $I$ is closed, so $A$ is complete for the quotient norm.
The quotient norm is submultiplicative, so $A$ is a [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) over $k$.
Being affinoid adds that $A$ is a quotient of a Tate algebra, which makes it Noetherian.
links.why: Banach algebra tools apply to affinoid algebras, which also have strong finiteness properties.

reminder: An algebraic equation sets a polynomial equal to zero.
definition: An algebraic equation over a [field](c:field) $k$ is an [equation](c:equation) $P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0$, where $P$ is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) with coefficients in $k$. A solution is a tuple of elements of $k$, or of a larger field, at which $P$ vanishes.
examples: The equation $x^2-2=0$ over $\mathbb Q$ has the solutions $\pm\sqrt2$ in $\mathbb R$ and no solution in $\mathbb Q$.
The equation $x^2+y^2-1=0$ over $\mathbb R$ has the unit circle as its set of solutions.
Non-example: the equation $\sin x=0$ is not algebraic, because $\sin$ is not a polynomial; its solutions $n\pi$ are infinite in number, and no nonzero polynomial vanishes at all of them.

steps: Take a [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0$, where $P$ has integer coefficients and we look for integer solutions.
The polynomial $P$ also has coefficients in the field $\mathbb Q$, so $P=0$ is an algebraic equation over $\mathbb Q$.
The Diophantine solutions are the solutions of this algebraic equation that lie in $\mathbb Z^n$.
The Diophantine case adds the condition that the solutions are integers.
links.why: Algebraic tools such as field extensions and varieties apply to Diophantine equations.

reminder: An algebraic group is a variety with multiplication and inverse maps that are morphisms of varieties and satisfy the group laws.
definition: Let $k$ be a field, usually [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field). An algebraic $k$-group is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of [algebraic varieties](c:algebraic-variety) over $k$: a variety $G$ with a neutral point and morphisms of varieties for multiplication and inverse that satisfy the laws of a [group](c:group).
examples: The general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n$, an affine variety given by $\det\ne0$, and its closed subgroup $\mathrm{SL}_n$.
The additive group $\mathbb G_a$ and the multiplicative group $\mathbb G_m$.
An elliptic curve with its group law is an algebraic group that is projective.
Non-example: the projective line $\mathbb P^1$ is a variety but has no algebraic group law, because a complete connected algebraic group is an abelian variety, and $\mathbb P^1$ is not one.

steps: Take an algebraic group $G$ with multiplication $m$, inverse $i$ and neutral point $e$.
These are morphisms in the category of varieties over $k$, and the group laws hold as equalities of morphisms.
So $G$ is a [group object](c:group-object) in the category of algebraic varieties over $k$.
The special case chooses varieties over $k$ as the ambient category.
links.why: The general theory of group objects, such as actions and quotients, applies to algebraic groups.

steps: Take a [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) $G$, an affine variety with group law morphisms.
Every affine variety is an algebraic variety, so $G$ is a group object in varieties.
So $G$ is an algebraic group.
The linear case adds that $G$ is affine, which is the same as being a closed subgroup of some $\mathrm{GL}_n$.
links.why: Results on algebraic groups apply to linear groups, and they also cover abelian varieties.

reminder: An algebraic structure is a set with operations, such as addition, that satisfy given equational laws.
definition: An algebraic structure consists of a [set](c:set) $A$ and a family of finitary operations, which are [functions](c:function) $A^n\to A$, usually required to satisfy equational [axioms](c:axiom). Groups, rings and lattices are algebraic structures.
examples: A group: a set with an associative multiplication, a neutral element and inverses.
A ring $(R,+,\cdot,0,1)$ with its distributive law.
A lattice: a set with two binary operations, meet and join, that satisfy the lattice laws.
Non-example: a topological space is a set with a family of open subsets, not a set with operations $A^n\to A$, so it is not an algebraic structure.

steps: Take a [group](c:group) $(G,\cdot,e,{}^{-1})$.
Its multiplication $G^2\to G$, its unit $G^0\to G$ and its inverse $G\to G$ are operations on the set $G$.
The group laws are equational axioms for these operations.
So $G$ is an algebraic structure with three operations and the group laws.
links.why: Notions made for all algebraic structures, such as homomorphisms and congruences, apply to groups.

reminder: An algebraic theory is a set of operation symbols with equations between terms; its models are the algebras that satisfy them.
definition: An algebraic theory is a [signature](c:signature-in-logic) of operation symbols, each with a finite arity, together with a set of [equations](c:equation) between terms built from these symbols. Its models are the sets with operations that satisfy all equations; they form a variety of algebras, and the theory is a special kind of theory in [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic).
examples: The theory of groups has the symbols $\cdot$, $e$ and ${}^{-1}$ and the equations of associativity, neutral element and inverse.
The theory of commutative rings with unit; its models are the commutative rings.
The theory of semilattices has one binary operation that is associative, commutative and idempotent.
Non-example: the theory of fields is not algebraic, because the axiom that every nonzero element has an inverse is not an equation, and a product of two fields is not a field.

steps: Take an algebraic theory $T$ with total operations given by symbols and equations.
Each operation is defined on all tuples, so its domain is cut out by the empty set of equations.
So $T$ is an [essentially algebraic theory](c:essentially-algebraic-theory) with no proper partial operation.
The algebraic case adds the condition that every operation is total.
links.why: Results for essentially algebraic theories, such as the existence of free models, apply to algebraic theories.

reminder: An alternating series has terms that change sign at every step.
definition: An alternating series is a [series](c:series) $\sum_{n=0}^\infty(-1)^na_n$ with $a_n>0$ for all $n$, so that consecutive terms have opposite signs.
examples: The Leibniz series $1-\tfrac13+\tfrac15-\tfrac17+\cdots$ has the sum $\pi/4$.
The alternating harmonic series $1-\tfrac12+\tfrac13-\cdots$ converges to $\ln2$.
Non-example: the series $1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\cdots$ has only positive terms, so it is not alternating.

steps: Take an alternating series $\sum(-1)^na_n$ with $a_n>0$.
The numbers $b_n=(-1)^na_n$ form a sequence, and the series is the sum of the $b_n$.
So it is a [series](c:series), defined through the partial sums of $(b_n)$.
The alternating case adds that the signs of $b_n$ alternate, which gives the Leibniz test: if $a_n$ decreases to $0$, the series converges.
links.why: Alternating series have a convergence test and an error bound that general series lack.

reminder: A divisor is ample when some positive multiple of it embeds the variety into projective space.
definition: A [divisor](c:divisor) $D$ on a [projective variety](c:projective-variety) $X$ is ample if its [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $\mathcal O_X(D)$ is [ample](c:ample-sheaf). Equivalently, for some $m>0$ the global sections of $\mathcal O_X(mD)$ give a closed embedding of $X$ into a projective space.
examples: A hyperplane section $H$ of a projective variety $X\subset\mathbb P^N$ is an ample divisor.
On a smooth projective curve, a divisor is ample exactly when its degree is positive.
On $\mathbb P^n$, a divisor is ample exactly when its degree is positive.
Non-example: on $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$, the divisor $D=\{pt\}\times\mathbb P^1$ is not ample, because $D\cdot D=0$, while an ample divisor on a surface has positive self-intersection.

steps: Take an ample divisor $D$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$.
Every curve $C$ in $X$ has $D\cdot C>0$, so in particular $D\cdot C\ge0$, and $D$ is nef.
Some multiple $mD$ is very ample, so $(mD)^n$ is the positive degree of $X$ in projective space, hence $D^n>0$ and $D$ is big.
So $D$ is [big and nef](c:big-and-nef-divisor); the ample case asks for the stronger condition $D\cdot C>0$ for every curve.
links.why: Theorems for big and nef divisors, such as vanishing theorems, apply to every ample divisor.

reminder: A line bundle is ample when some positive tensor power of it gives an embedding into projective space.
definition: A [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ on a scheme $X$ of finite type over a field is ample if, for some $m>0$, the [global sections](c:global-section) of $L^{\otimes m}$ give an embedding of $X$ into a projective space; that is, $L^{\otimes m}$ is [very ample](c:very-ample-line-bundle). On a complex projective variety, this holds exactly when the Chern class of $L$ is represented by a Kähler form.
examples: The line bundle $\mathcal O(1)$ on $\mathbb P^n$ is ample, and even very ample.
On a smooth projective curve, a line bundle is ample exactly when its degree is positive.
On a complex projective variety, a line bundle is ample exactly when its first Chern class is represented by a Kähler form.
Non-example: the trivial bundle $\mathcal O_X$ on a projective variety $X$ of positive dimension is not ample, because its global sections are constants and give no embedding.

steps: Take a [very ample line bundle](c:very-ample-line-bundle) $L$ on $X$, so its global sections give an embedding $X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^N$.
Take $m=1$ in the definition of an ample line bundle.
Then $L^{\otimes1}=L$ is very ample, so $L$ is ample.
The ample case also allows a higher power $L^{\otimes m}$, so it is the more general condition.
links.why: A result about ample line bundles applies to every very ample one, and ampleness is easier to test.

steps: Take an ample line bundle $L$ on $X$.
By definition $L$ is a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on $X$.
The ample case adds a positivity condition: some power of $L$ has enough global sections to embed $X$ in projective space.
links.why: Ample line bundles carry the positivity that gives vanishing theorems and projective embeddings.

reminder: An analytic family of operators depends holomorphically on a complex parameter, with a norm-convergent power series near each parameter value.
definition: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be an open set and let $X$ and $Y$ be [Banach spaces](c:banach-space). An analytic family of operators is a map $z\mapsto A(z)$ from $\Omega$ to the [bounded operators](c:bounded-operator) from $X$ to $Y$ such that near each $z_0\in\Omega$ it is a norm-convergent [power series](c:power-series) $A(z)=\sum_nA_n(z-z_0)^n$ with $A_n$ bounded operators.
examples: The family $A(z)=A_0+zA_1$ for two bounded operators $A_0$ and $A_1$.
The resolvent $z\mapsto(T-z)^{-1}$ of a bounded operator $T$ is an analytic family on the complement of the spectrum of $T$.
The family $z\mapsto I-zK$ for a compact operator $K$ is analytic on $\mathbb C$; the analytic Fredholm theorem says it is invertible except on a discrete set.
Non-example: the family $z\mapsto\bar z\,I$ is not analytic, because it is not complex differentiable.

steps: Take a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$.
View the number $f(z)$ as the operator on the one-dimensional space $\mathbb C$ that multiplies by $f(z)$.
Then $z\mapsto f(z)$ is a map into the bounded operators on $\mathbb C$, given near each point by a convergent power series.
So $f$ is an analytic family of operators on $\mathbb C$.
links.why: Complex analysis carries over to operator families, so tools such as Cauchy's formula still apply.

reminder: An ancillary statistic is a function of the data whose distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter.
definition: Let $X$ be data drawn from a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $P_\theta$ that depends on a parameter $\theta$. A [statistic](c:statistic) $T(X)$ is ancillary if the distribution of $T(X)$ is the same for every value of $\theta$.
examples: For independent $N(\theta,1)$ data $X_1,\dots,X_n$, the sample variance is ancillary, because $(n-1)S^2$ has the $\chi^2_{n-1}$ distribution for every $\theta$.
In a location family, the range $X_{(n)}-X_{(1)}$ of the sample is ancillary.
Non-example: the sample mean $\bar X$ of $N(\theta,1)$ data is not ancillary, because its distribution $N(\theta,1/n)$ depends on $\theta$.

steps: Take an ancillary statistic $T$, a function of the data $X$.
So $T$ is a [statistic](c:statistic).
The ancillary case adds that the distribution of $T(X)$ is the same for every parameter value.
links.why: An ancillary statistic carries no information about the parameter, which is the basis of Basu's theorem.

reminder: The annihilator of a subset of a vector space is the set of linear functionals that vanish on it.
definition: Let $X$ be a [vector space](c:vector-space) and $M$ a [subset](c:subset) of $X$. The annihilator of $M$ is the set $M^\perp$ of [linear functionals](c:linear-functional) $f$ on $X$ with $f(m)=0$ for all $m\in M$; it is a subspace of the [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$.
examples: In $\mathbb R^3$, let $M$ be the span of $e_1$; then $M^\perp$ is the set of functionals $f=(a,b,c)$ with $a=0$, a plane in $(\mathbb R^3)^*$.
For every space $X$, $\{0\}^\perp=X^*$ and $X^\perp=\{0\}$.
For a bounded operator $T:X\to Y$ between Banach spaces, $\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp$.
Non-example: for $M=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}$ in $\mathbb R^3$, the functional $e_1^*$ is not in $M^\perp$, because $e_1^*(e_1)=1$.

reminder: An antilinear map is additive and sends multiplication by a scalar $c$ to multiplication by its complex conjugate.
definition: Let $V$ and $W$ be [complex vector spaces](c:complex-vector-space). A map $f:V\to W$ is antilinear if $f(u+v)=f(u)+f(v)$ and $f(cv)=\bar c\,f(v)$ for all $u,v\in V$ and all complex numbers $c$. More generally, over a ring with an [involution](c:involution), the conjugate $\bar c$ is replaced by the image of $c$ under the involution.
examples: Complex conjugation $z\mapsto\bar z$ on $\mathbb C$, seen as a complex vector space, is antilinear.
On $\mathbb C^n$, conjugating each coordinate is antilinear.
On a Hilbert space with an inner product that is linear in the first slot, the map $v\mapsto\langle\cdot,v\rangle$ into the dual space is antilinear.
Non-example: the identity map of $\mathbb C$ is linear but not antilinear, because $\mathrm{id}(i\cdot1)=i$ and $\bar i\,\mathrm{id}(1)=-i$.

steps: Take a ring homomorphism $\sigma:R\to S$ and recall that a $\sigma$-[semilinear map](c:semilinear-map) satisfies $f(cv)=\sigma(c)f(v)$.
Take $R=S=\mathbb C$ and let $\sigma(c)=\bar c$, which is a ring automorphism of $\mathbb C$.
Then a $\sigma$-semilinear map is additive and satisfies $f(cv)=\bar c\,f(v)$.
That is an antilinear map, so antilinear maps are the semilinear maps for complex conjugation.
links.why: Facts about semilinear maps, such as the structure of their kernels, apply to antilinear maps.

reminder: An arborescence is a directed graph with a root from which there is exactly one directed path to every vertex.
definition: An arborescence with root $r$ is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph) in which, for every [vertex](c:vertex) $v$, there is exactly one directed [path](c:path) from $r$ to $v$.
examples: A rooted tree with every edge directed away from the root, such as a family tree with arrows from parent to child.
The graph with vertices $r,a,b$ and edges $r\to a$ and $r\to b$.
A single vertex with no edge.
Non-example: the graph with edges $r\to a$, $r\to b$ and $a\to b$ has two paths from $r$ to $b$, so it is not an arborescence.

steps: Take an arborescence $A$ with root $r$.
It consists of vertices and directed edges, so it is a [directed graph](c:directed-graph).
The arborescence adds that from $r$ there is exactly one directed path to each vertex.
links.why: Arborescences are the directed graphs used to count Eulerian circuits in the BEST theorem.

reminder: An arithmetic Chow group refines the Chow group of an arithmetic scheme by adding Green currents on its complex points.
definition: For a [regular scheme](c:regular-scheme) $X$ that is flat and projective over $\mathbb Z$, the arithmetic Chow group $\widehat{CH}^p(X)$ is the group of pairs $(Z,g)$, where $Z$ is a codimension $p$ [algebraic cycle](c:algebraic-cycle) on $X$ and $g$ is a Green current for $Z$ on the complex points $X(\mathbb C)$, modulo the pairs that come from rational functions and from exact forms. It refines the [Chow group](c:chow-group) in the same way that ordinary differential cohomology refines ordinary cohomology.
examples: For $X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$, the group $\widehat{CH}^1(X)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$, and the isomorphism gives the arithmetic degree.
A line bundle with a Hermitian metric on $X$ gives a class $(\operatorname{div}s,-\log\|s\|^2)$ in $\widehat{CH}^1(X)$, for a rational section $s$.
Non-example: the ordinary Chow group $CH^p(X)$ is not arithmetic; its classes carry no Green currents, so a cycle $Z$ alone is not a class of $\widehat{CH}^p(X)$.

reminder: The arrow category of $C$ has the morphisms of $C$ as objects and commutative squares as morphisms.
definition: The arrow category $\mathrm{Arr}(C)$ of a [category](c:category) $C$ has the morphisms of $C$ as objects. A morphism from $f:a\to b$ to $g:c\to d$ is a pair $(u:a\to c,\ v:b\to d)$ that makes the [commutative square](c:comm-sq) $g\circ u=v\circ f$ commute, and [composition](c:composition) is done componentwise.
examples: In $\mathrm{Arr}(\mathrm{Set})$, an object is a function $f:A\to B$, and a morphism from $f$ to $g$ is a pair of functions that make the square commute.
Domain and codomain give two functors $\mathrm{Arr}(C)\to C$, and the identity arrows give a functor $C\to\mathrm{Arr}(C)$.
The arrow category is the [functor category](c:functor-category) from the category $\{0\to1\}$ to $C$.
Non-example: a pair of morphisms $(u,v)$ with $g\circ u\ne v\circ f$ is not a morphism of $\mathrm{Arr}(C)$, because its square does not commute.

steps: Let $\mathbf 2$ be the category with objects $0,1$ and one non-identity arrow $0\to1$.
A functor $\mathbf 2\to C$ picks two objects of $C$ and one arrow between them, that is, a morphism of $C$.
A natural transformation between two such functors is a pair of arrows that make the naturality square commute.
So $\mathrm{Arr}(C)$ is the [functor category](c:functor-category) from $\mathbf 2$ to $C$, a special case with a fixed source.
links.why: General facts about functor categories, such as limits computed pointwise, apply to arrow categories.

reminder: A ring is Artinian when every descending chain of ideals becomes constant.
definition: A [ring](c:ring) $R$ is (left) Artinian if every descending chain $I_1\supseteq I_2\supseteq\cdots$ of left [ideals](c:ideal) of $R$ is eventually constant, that is, if the left ideals satisfy the [descending chain condition](c:descending-chain-condition).
examples: Every field and every finite ring, such as $\mathbb Z/n$, is Artinian.
A finite-dimensional algebra over a field, such as $k[x]/(x^n)$ or the ring of $n\times n$ matrices over $k$, is Artinian.
Non-example: the ring $\mathbb Z$ is not Artinian, because the chain $(2)\supsetneq(4)\supsetneq(8)\supsetneq\cdots$ never becomes constant.

steps: Take an Artinian ring $R$ with Jacobson radical $J$.
By the Hopkins-Levitzki theorem, $J$ is nilpotent and $R/J$ is semisimple.
Each factor $J^i/J^{i+1}$ is a module of finite length, so $R$ has finite length as a module over itself.
A module of finite length satisfies the ascending chain condition, so $R$ is a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring).
links.why: Finiteness results for Noetherian rings, such as the Hilbert basis theorem, apply to Artinian rings.

steps: Take a [semisimple ring](c:semisimple-ring) $R$, so $R$ is a finite direct sum of simple left ideals.
A module with a finite composition series has finite length.
So every chain of left ideals of $R$ is eventually constant, and $R$ is left Artinian.
The converse fails: $k[x]/(x^2)$ is Artinian but not semisimple.
links.why: Results for Artinian rings, such as the structure of the radical, apply to every semisimple ring.

reminder: A partially ordered set satisfies the ascending chain condition when every ascending sequence of its elements is eventually constant.
definition: A [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) satisfies the ascending chain condition if every ascending [sequence](c:sequence) $x_0\le x_1\le x_2\le\cdots$ is eventually constant. For an object $B$ of a category, the condition is applied to the poset of [subobjects](c:subobject) of $B$.
examples: Every finite poset satisfies the ascending chain condition.
The ideals of $\mathbb Z$, ordered by inclusion, satisfy it, because $\mathbb Z$ is Noetherian.
The natural numbers with the reversed order $\ge$ satisfy it, because a decreasing sequence of natural numbers stops.
Non-example: the natural numbers with the usual order do not satisfy it, because the sequence $0<1<2<\cdots$ never becomes constant.

steps: Take a ring $R$ and the poset of its ideals, ordered by inclusion.
A ring is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring) when every ascending chain of ideals $I_0\subseteq I_1\subseteq\cdots$ becomes constant.
That is exactly the ascending chain condition for this poset.
So the Noetherian rings are the rings whose poset of ideals satisfies the ascending chain condition.
links.why: A result proved for the ascending chain condition on any poset applies to Noetherian rings and Noetherian modules.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ and the set of its principal ideals, ordered by inclusion.
This set is a poset.
The condition on principal ideals says that every ascending chain $(a_0)\subseteq(a_1)\subseteq\cdots$ becomes constant.
That is the ascending chain condition for this poset.
links.why: Arguments about chains in any poset apply to principal ideals, for example in the proof that a domain has factorizations.

reminder: An operation is associative when $(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$ for all $a$, $b$ and $c$.
definition: A [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $\cdot$ on a [set](c:set) $S$ is associative if $(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$ for all $a,b,c\in S$.
examples: Addition and multiplication of real numbers are associative.
Composition of functions is associative.
Concatenation of words is associative.
Non-example: subtraction on $\mathbb Z$ is not associative, because $(3-2)-1=0$ but $3-(2-1)=2$.

steps: Take a set $S$ with an associative operation $\cdot$.
By definition $\cdot$ is a [binary operation](c:binary-operation), a function $S\times S\to S$.
The associative case adds that $(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)$ for all $a,b,c$.
So brackets do not matter, and a product $a_1\cdot\ldots\cdot a_n$ is well defined.
links.why: Associativity lets a learner drop brackets in long products and argue by induction on their length.

reminder: An asymptotically flat manifold looks like Euclidean space far away from a compact set.
definition: A [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(M^n,g)$ is asymptotically flat if, outside a [compact](c:compact-space) set, $M$ is a finite union of ends, and each end is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$ minus a ball. In the coordinates $x$ of each end, the metric satisfies $g_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=O(|x|^{-\tau})$ for some $\tau>0$, with matching decay of its derivatives, where $\delta$ is the metric of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
examples: Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$ with its standard metric.
The time-symmetric slice of the Schwarzschild spacetime, $g=(1+\tfrac m{2r})^4\delta$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, which has two asymptotically flat ends.
Any metric on $\mathbb R^n$ that equals the Euclidean metric outside a ball.

Non-example: hyperbolic space is not asymptotically flat, because its curvature is $-1$ everywhere and no coordinates make $g$ tend to $\delta$ at infinity; the round sphere is not either, because it is compact and has no end.

steps: Take an asymptotically flat manifold $(M,g)$.
Then $M$ is a smooth manifold with a Riemannian metric $g$.
So $(M,g)$ is a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold).
The asymptotically flat case adds that $g$ tends to the Euclidean metric along each end.
links.why: Riemannian tools such as curvature apply, and the decay at infinity allows a definition of total mass.

steps: Take Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$ with its standard metric $\delta$.
It is a Riemannian manifold with one end, outside any ball.
In the standard coordinates $g_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=0$, which is $O(|x|^{-\tau})$ for every $\tau$.
So $\mathbb R^n$ is asymptotically flat, and its mass is zero.
links.why: Euclidean space is the model case, and every asymptotically flat manifold compares with it at infinity.

reminder: An asymptotically flat spacetime approaches Minkowski spacetime far from any source.
definition: A [spacetime](c:spacetime) is asymptotically flat if, far from a bounded region, its metric in suitable coordinates differs from the [Minkowski metric](c:minkowski-metric) by terms that decay as the distance $r\to\infty$, for example like $O(r^{-1})$. A common formal version asks that a spacelike hypersurface is [asymptotically flat](c:asymptotically-flat-manifold) and that its extrinsic curvature decays.
examples: Minkowski spacetime itself.
The Schwarzschild spacetime of a non-rotating black hole, whose metric tends to the Minkowski metric as $r\to\infty$.
The [Kerr spacetime](c:kerr-spacetime) of a rotating black hole is asymptotically flat.
Non-example: de Sitter spacetime has constant positive curvature and stays curved at infinity, so it is not asymptotically flat; anti de Sitter spacetime is not either.

steps: Take an asymptotically flat spacetime $(M,g)$.
It is a manifold with a Lorentzian metric $g$, so it is a [spacetime](c:spacetime).
The asymptotically flat case adds that far out, $g$ approaches the Minkowski metric.
links.why: General relativity applies, and the decay at infinity lets a learner define conserved quantities such as mass.

steps: Take [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) with its metric $\eta$.
In standard coordinates the metric is $\eta$ everywhere, so the difference from $\eta$ is zero.
Zero decays faster than every power of $r^{-1}$.
So Minkowski space is asymptotically flat.
links.why: Minkowski space is the model case that every asymptotically flat spacetime approaches.

reminder: An atom of a poset is a minimal element among the elements that are not the least element.
definition: Let $(P,\le)$ be a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) with a least element $0$, the [bottom element](c:bottom). An atom of $P$ is an element $a\ne0$ such that no element $x$ satisfies $0<x<a$.
examples: In the subsets of a set, ordered by inclusion, the atoms are the one-element subsets.
In the divisors of $n$, ordered by divisibility, the atoms are the primes that divide $n$.
In a measure algebra, an atom is a class of sets of positive measure such that every measurable subset has measure zero or the full measure of the set.
Non-example: in the Boolean algebra of Lebesgue measurable subsets of $[0,1]$ modulo null sets, there is no atom, because every set of positive measure splits into two parts of positive measure.

reminder: An automorphic form is a function on a Lie group that is invariant under a discrete subgroup and satisfies finiteness and growth conditions.
definition: Let $G$ be a semisimple [Lie group](c:lie-group) with maximal compact subgroup $K$, and let $\Gamma\subset G$ be an arithmetic [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup). An automorphic form is a smooth function $f:G\to\mathbb C$ with $f(\gamma g)=f(g)$ for all $\gamma\in\Gamma$, such that $f$ is $K$-finite, is annihilated by an ideal of finite codimension in the center of the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) of the Lie algebra of $G$, and has moderate growth.
examples: A modular form of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ gives an automorphic form on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ by the lift $\phi_f(g)=f(g\cdot i)(ci+d)^{-k}$.
A Maass form, an eigenfunction of the hyperbolic Laplacian on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathbb H$ with moderate growth, gives an automorphic form.
An Eisenstein series for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ is an automorphic form that is not a cusp form.

Non-example: a nonzero smooth bump function on $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$ supported in a small open set is $\Gamma$-invariant but not automorphic, because automorphic forms are real analytic and cannot vanish on an open set unless they are zero.

steps: Take a [modular form](c:modular-form) $f$ of weight $k$ for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$.
Define $\phi_f(g)=f(g\cdot i)(ci+d)^{-k}$ for $g=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)$.
The function $\phi_f$ is left $\Gamma$-invariant, because $f$ transforms with weight $k$ under $\Gamma$.
It is $K$-finite, an eigenfunction of the Casimir operator and of moderate growth, so it is an automorphic form.
links.why: Results about automorphic forms apply to modular forms, and they also cover other groups.

reminder: An automorphic representation is an irreducible representation of an adelic group that occurs in the space of automorphic forms.
definition: Let $G$ be a reductive group over a number field $F$ and let $\mathbb A$ be the [ring of adeles](c:ring-of-adeles) of $F$. An automorphic representation of $G(\mathbb A)$ is an [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation) that occurs as a subquotient of the space of [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) on $G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb A)$.
examples: For $G=\mathrm{GL}_1$ over $\mathbb Q$, the automorphic representations are the Hecke characters.
A Hecke eigenform that is a cusp form generates an automorphic representation of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})$.
The constant functions on $G(F)\backslash G(\mathbb A)$ span a one-dimensional automorphic representation.

Non-example: a supercuspidal representation of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)$ is a representation of a local group, so it is not automorphic by itself, although it can be a local factor of an automorphic representation.

steps: Take an automorphic representation $\pi$ of $G(\mathbb A)$.
The space of automorphic forms carries an action of the Hecke algebra of $G(\mathbb A)$, and $\pi$ is an irreducible subquotient of it.
So $\pi$ is an [irreducible representation](c:irreducible-representation) of that action.
The automorphic case adds that $\pi$ occurs in the space of automorphic forms.
links.why: Tools for irreducible representations, such as tensor product decompositions into local factors, apply to automorphic representations.

reminder: The automorphism group of an object is the group of its invertible self-maps that preserve the structure, under composition.
definition: The automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(X)$ of an object $X$ in a [category](c:category) is the set of all [automorphisms](c:automorphism) of $X$, with [composition](c:composition) as the product. It is a [group](c:group) with the identity map as neutral element.
examples: For a set $X$ with $n$ elements, $\operatorname{Aut}(X)$ in the category of sets is the symmetric group $S_n$.
For a vector space $V$, $\operatorname{Aut}(V)$ is the general linear group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$.
For the cyclic group $\mathbb Z/n$, $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Z/n)\cong(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$.
Non-example: the set of all endomorphisms of a vector space $V\neq0$ is not a group under composition, because non-invertible maps have no inverse.

steps: Take a Galois extension $L/K$ of fields.
Consider the field automorphisms of $L$ that fix every element of $K$.
These are the automorphisms of $L$ in the category of $K$-algebras, so they form the group $\operatorname{Aut}(L/K)$.
The [Galois group](c:galois-group) is this group, so it is an automorphism group.
links.why: Facts about automorphism groups, such as the action on the object, apply to Galois groups.

steps: Take a smooth manifold $M$ in the category of smooth manifolds and smooth maps.
An automorphism of $M$ in this category is a smooth map with a smooth inverse, that is, a diffeomorphism.
So $\operatorname{Aut}(M)$ is the group of diffeomorphisms of $M$.
Thus the [diffeomorphism group](c:diffeomorphism-group) is the automorphism group for smooth manifolds.
links.why: Facts about automorphism groups apply to diffeomorphism groups of manifolds.

reminder: An axiom is a proposition that a theory requires to be true, and from which other theorems are proved.
definition: An axiom of a [theory](c:theory) is a [proposition](c:proposition) in the [language](c:language) of the theory that every [model](c:model) of the theory must satisfy. It is a starting point of [deduction](c:deduction) and is not proved inside the theory.
examples: Associativity $x(yz)=(xy)z$ is an axiom of the theory of groups; a non-associative operation is not a model.
Extensionality is an axiom of set theory: two sets with the same elements are equal.
The parallel postulate is an axiom of Euclidean geometry; replacing it gives hyperbolic geometry.
Non-example: the Pythagorean theorem is not an axiom of Euclidean geometry in Hilbert's axiomatization, because it is proved from the axioms.

steps: Take an axiom $A$ of a theory $T$.
By definition $A$ is a [proposition](c:proposition) in the language of $T$.
The axiom adds that every model of $T$ must satisfy $A$, and that proofs in $T$ may use $A$ without proof.
links.why: An axiom is an ordinary proposition that a theory chooses to assume.

reminder: The image of a set under a definable function is again a set.
definition: The axiom schema of replacement says: let $\varphi(x,y)$ be a [formula](c:formula), possibly with parameters, and let $A$ be a [set](c:set). If for every $x\in A$ there is exactly one $y$ with $\varphi(x,y)$, then $\{y:\exists x\in A\ \varphi(x,y)\}$ is a set. It is one [axiom schema](c:axiom-schema), with one instance for each formula $\varphi$.
examples: Replacement proves that $\{\omega,\mathcal P(\omega),\mathcal P(\mathcal P(\omega)),\dots\}$ is a set; Zermelo's axioms without replacement do not prove it.
Replacement proves that every well-ordered set is isomorphic to a unique von Neumann ordinal, as in Mostowski's collapsing lemma.
Non-example: the formula $x<y$ on $\mathbb N$ is not covered, because each $x$ has many $y$ with $x<y$; replacement needs exactly one $y$ for each $x$.

steps: Take a set $A$ and a formula $\psi(x)$, and look for the subset $\{x\in A:\psi(x)\}$; if it is empty, the empty set works, so pick $a\in A$ with $\psi(a)$.
Let $\varphi(x,y)$ say: ($\psi(x)$ and $y=x$) or ($\neg\psi(x)$ and $y=a$).
For each $x\in A$ there is exactly one $y$ with $\varphi(x,y)$, so replacement gives the set of all these $y$.
This set equals $\{x\in A:\psi(x)\}$, because $a$ already satisfies $\psi$, so it is an instance of [separation](c:axiom-of-separation).
links.why: Once replacement is available, separation is a consequence, so replacement is the stronger axiom.

reminder: A collection of coalitions is balanced when positive weights on its members give every player total weight exactly 1.
definition: Let $N$ be a finite set of players of a [cooperative game](c:cooperative-game). A collection $\mathcal B$ of nonempty [subsets](c:subset) of $N$, called coalitions, is balanced if there are positive weights $(\lambda_S)_{S\in\mathcal B}$ such that $\sum_{S\in\mathcal B,\ i\in S}\lambda_S=1$ for every player $i\in N$.
examples: Every partition of $N$ into coalitions is balanced, with all weights equal to $1$.
For $N=\{1,2,3\}$, the collection $\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\}$ is balanced with all weights $\tfrac12$, because each player lies in two coalitions.
Non-example: the collection $\{\{1,2\},\{1,3\}\}$ on $N=\{1,2,3\}$ is not balanced, because players $2$ and $3$ force $\lambda_{12}=\lambda_{13}=1$, and then player $1$ has total weight $2$.

steps: Take a [partition](c:set-partition) $\mathcal P$ of $N$ into nonempty blocks.
Give every block the weight $1$.
Each player lies in exactly one block, so the weights of the blocks that contain this player add up to $1$.
So $\mathcal P$ is a balanced collection; balanced collections are the fractional version of partitions.
links.why: The Bondareva-Shapley theorem uses balanced collections as the fractional partitions that test whether a game has a nonempty core.

reminder: A band-limited signal has a Fourier transform that vanishes outside a bounded interval of frequencies.
definition: A signal $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ that is a [square integrable function](c:square-integrable-function) is band-limited if its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) has bounded [support](c:support-of-a-function); that is, there is $B>0$ with $\hat f(\xi)=0$ for $|\xi|>B$.
examples: The function $\operatorname{sinc}(t)=\sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)$ has the Fourier transform $\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$, so it is band-limited.
The function $\operatorname{sinc}^2$ has a triangle function on $[-1,1]$ as Fourier transform, so it is band-limited.
By the Nyquist-Shannon theorem, a signal with bandwidth $B$ is determined by its samples at spacing $1/(2B)$.

Non-example: a nonzero signal that is zero outside a bounded time interval is not band-limited, because its Fourier transform is an entire function and cannot vanish on an interval of frequencies unless it is zero.

reminder: The Bargmann-Fock space is the Hilbert space of holomorphic functions that are square integrable for a Gaussian weight.
definition: The Bargmann-Fock space $\mathcal F(\mathbb C^n)$ is the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) $f:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C$ with $\int|f(z)|^2e^{-|z|^2}\,d\lambda(z)<\infty$, where $\lambda$ is [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). Its inner product is $\langle f,g\rangle=\pi^{-n}\int f\bar g\,e^{-|z|^2}\,d\lambda(z)$.
examples: The monomials $z^\alpha/\sqrt{\alpha!}$ form an orthonormal basis, with $\alpha!=\alpha_1!\cdots\alpha_n!$.
The constant function $1$ is the vacuum vector, and the kernel functions $e^{\langle z,w\rangle}$ reproduce values: $f(w)=\langle f,e^{\langle\cdot,w\rangle}\rangle$.
Every polynomial belongs to the space, because Gaussian integrals of polynomials are finite.
Non-example: the entire function $e^{z^2}$ on $\mathbb C$ is not in the space, because $|e^{z^2}|^2e^{-|z|^2}=e^{x^2-3y^2}$ has an infinite integral.

steps: Take the space $\mathcal F$ of holomorphic functions with finite Gaussian-weighted norm.
The formula $\langle f,g\rangle=\pi^{-n}\int f\bar g\,e^{-|z|^2}\,d\lambda$ is a positive definite inner product on $\mathcal F$.
Point evaluations are bounded, so a Cauchy sequence converges locally uniformly to a holomorphic function, which lies in $\mathcal F$.
So $\mathcal F$ is complete, hence a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), whose elements are holomorphic functions.
links.why: Hilbert space tools apply, and the reproducing kernel makes point evaluation a bounded linear functional.

reminder: The base-$p$ digits of a natural number are the unique coefficients $d_i$ with $0\le d_i<p$ and $n=\sum d_ip^i$.
definition: Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, for example a [prime number](c:prime-number), and let $n$ be a [natural number](c:natural-number). The base-$p$ digits of $n$ are the unique integers $d_0,\dots,d_k$ with $0\le d_i<p$ and $d_k\ne0$ such that $n=\sum_{i=0}^kd_ip^i$.
examples: The base-$2$ digits of $13$ are $1,1,0,1$ (from highest to lowest), because $13=8+4+0+1$.
The base-$3$ digits of $37$ are $1,1,0,1$, because $37=27+9+0+1$.
By Kummer's theorem, the exponent of $p$ in $\binom{m+n}{m}$ is the number of carries when $m$ and $n$ are added in base $p$; for $p=2$ and $m=n=1$, one carry gives $\binom21=2$.
Non-example: the string $1,3,0$ is not a list of base-$3$ digits, because the digit $3$ is not less than $3$.

reminder: The Beck-Chevalley condition says that the canonical comparison map between two ways of combining adjoints and base change is an isomorphism.
definition: Take a [commutative square](c:comm-sq) $f\circ p=g\circ q$ in a category $\mathcal B$ and an indexed category $\mathcal E$ whose reindexing functors $u^*$ all have [left adjoints](c:adjoint-functor) $u_!$. The square satisfies the Beck-Chevalley condition if the [mate](c:mate) $q_!p^*\Rightarrow g^*f_!$ of the [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism) $p^*f^*\cong q^*g^*$ is itself a natural isomorphism. In the usual case, the square is a pullback.
examples: Let $\mathcal E(X)=\mathrm{Set}/X$, with $u^*$ the pullback functor and $u_!$ composition with $u$; every pullback square of sets satisfies the condition, by the pasting law for pullbacks.
Let $\mathcal E(X)$ be the subsets of $X$, with $u^*$ the preimage and $u_!$ the direct image; for a pullback square of sets, $g^{-1}(f(A))=q(p^{-1}(A))$ for $A\subseteq X$.

Non-example: take $P=\emptyset$ and $X=Y=Z=\{*\}$ with identity maps $f$ and $g$, and use subsets; the square commutes but is not a pullback, and for $A=X$ we get $g^{-1}(f(A))=\{*\}$ while $q(p^{-1}(A))=\emptyset$.

reminder: A Bell state is one of four maximally entangled states of two qubits.
definition: A Bell state is one of the four maximally [entangled](c:entanglement) [quantum states](c:quantum-state) of two [qubits](c:qbit): $|\Phi^\pm\rangle=(|00\rangle\pm|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $|\Psi^\pm\rangle=(|01\rangle\pm|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
examples: The state $|\Phi^+\rangle=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives equal results on the two qubits when both are measured in the computational basis, each result with probability $\tfrac12$.
The singlet $|\Psi^-\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives opposite results when both qubits are measured in the same basis.
A [Hadamard gate](c:hadamard-gate) on the first qubit of $|00\rangle$, followed by a [CNOT gate](c:cnot-gate) with the first qubit as control, produces $|\Phi^+\rangle$.
Non-example: the product state $(|00\rangle+|01\rangle)/\sqrt2=|0\rangle|+\rangle$ is not entangled, so it is not a Bell state.

steps: Take a Bell state, for example $|\Phi^+\rangle=(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
It is a unit vector in the space $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$.
A unit vector defines a [pure state](c:pure-state).
The Bell state adds that the pair is maximally entangled: each qubit alone is in the maximally mixed state.
links.why: Bell states are the standard pure states that show entanglement, as in teleportation and Bell tests.

reminder: A Bernoulli distribution gives probability $p$ to the outcome 1 and probability $1-p$ to the outcome 0.
definition: For $0\le p\le1$, the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p$ is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on $\{0,1\}$ that gives the value $1$ probability $p$ and the value $0$ probability $1-p$. A [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with this distribution has $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$.
examples: A fair coin toss, with heads coded as $1$, has the Bernoulli distribution with $p=\tfrac12$.
The indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ of an event $A$ with $P(A)=p$ is a Bernoulli random variable with parameter $p$.
A Bernoulli random variable has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)$.
Non-example: the roll of a fair die has six outcomes, so it is not Bernoulli, because a Bernoulli variable takes only the values $0$ and $1$.

steps: Take the [binomial distribution](c:binomial-distribution) $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the law of the number of successes in $n$ independent trials with success probability $p$.
Set $n=1$, so there is only one trial.
The number of successes is $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.
That is the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p$.
links.why: The binomial distribution is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, so Bernoulli facts feed into binomial facts.

reminder: A Bernoulli scheme is the shift on sequences of independent identically distributed symbols, with the product measure.
definition: A Bernoulli scheme is a [measure-preserving system](c:measure-preserving-system) $(A^{\mathbb Z},\mu,T)$, where $A$ is a finite or countable set, $\mu$ is the [product measure](c:product-measure) of one [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\pi$ on $A$, and $T$ is the [shift](c:shift-map) $(Tx)_n=x_{n+1}$. Each coordinate is an independent copy of a random symbol with law $\pi$.
examples: Fair coin tossing: $A=\{0,1\}$ and $\pi=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ give the $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ Bernoulli scheme.

The scheme with $\pi=(\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$ and the scheme with $\pi=(\tfrac12,\tfrac18,\tfrac18,\tfrac18,\tfrac18)$ have the same entropy, so they are isomorphic by Ornstein's theorem.
The one-sided version uses $A^{\mathbb N}$ and the same shift, and it is not invertible.
Non-example: the shift on a stationary Markov chain with dependent steps is measure-preserving, but its measure is not a product measure, so it is not a Bernoulli scheme.

steps: Take a Bernoulli scheme $(A^{\mathbb Z},\mu,T)$.
The product measure $\mu$ is a probability measure, and the shift $T$ preserves it, because the coordinates are identically distributed.
So the triple is a [measure-preserving system](c:measure-preserving-system).
The Bernoulli case adds that the coordinates are independent.
links.why: Ergodic theory applies to Bernoulli schemes, which are the model of fully random behavior.

steps: Take the [Bernoulli distribution](c:bernoulli-distribution) with parameter $p$ on $\{0,1\}$.
The Bernoulli scheme is then the shift on sequences of independent Bernoulli trials.
A scheme with more symbols is the general case, with an arbitrary distribution $\pi$ in place of the two-point law.
links.why: A coin-tossing sequence is a Bernoulli scheme, so results on schemes apply to repeated independent trials.
